subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Time, Temperature, and Turbulence
description: A fast breakdown of Time, Temperature, and Turbulence for builders.

hook.text: Three variables control extraction: how long, how hot, and how much agitation the water gets.

buildup.text: Longer brew time extracts more. An espresso runs 25 seconds; cold brew steeps 12–24 hours.

discovery.text: Hotter water extracts faster. The ideal range is 90–96°C. Boiling water scorches and over-extracts.

twist.text: Cold brew breaks the rules—low temperature plus extreme time produces a smooth, low-acid concentrate.

climax.text: Stirring or pouring (turbulence) speeds extraction. A French press gets agitated; drip coffee doesn't.

punchline.text: Three dials, infinite results. Brewing is applied physics.

quiz.question: What is the ideal water temperature for brewing coffee?

details.summary: Brewing coffee involves three interacting variables: contact time between water and grounds, water temperature, and agitation or turbulence. Hotter water and more agitation speed extraction, while longer time compensates for coarser grinds or lower temperatures.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding these three levers gives you control over any brew method. When something tastes off, adjusting one of these variables is usually the fix.
takeaways: Hotter water extracts faster but risks bitterness
Longer brew time compensates for coarser grinds
Agitation speeds extraction and improves evenness

faq.question: What is the ideal water temperature for brewing coffee?
faq.answer: The SCA recommends 92 to 96 degrees Celsius for most methods. Lighter roasts often benefit from hotter water near 96 degrees. Darker roasts can taste better at lower temperatures around 88 to 90 degrees. Cold brew uses room temperature or refrigerator cold.

faq.question: What does agitation do during brewing?
faq.answer: Stirring or pouring turbulently moves fresh water against coffee grounds, replacing saturated water and maintaining the concentration gradient that drives extraction. Too much agitation can cause over-extraction. Pour-over technique largely controls this variable.
